analytic.title: Radar Dwell Scheduling Considering Physical Characteristics of Phased Array Antenna

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: This paper proposes novel techniques for scheduling radar dwells in phased array radar systems. In order to handle complex physical characteristics such as dwell interleaving, transmitting duty cycle constraint, and energy constraint, we propose a notion of schedulability envelope. The schedulability envelope designed offline hides the details of complex radar dwell scheduling and provides a simple measure for the schedulability check. Using the schedulability envelope, the proposed technique can efficiently perform the admission control for dynamic target tracking tasks. The simulation results show that the proposed approach can significantly improve the system utilization by taking advantage of dwell interleaving while guaranteeing the schedulability and physical constraints.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: A modern radar system employs a phased array antenna that can steer the radar beam electronically. Thanks to the electronic beam steering, the radar system can serve multifunctions such as searching surveillance space and tracking multiple targets at the same time. In order to perform such multiple functions, many radar beam steering commands, called radar dwells issued by search and track tasks, must be scheduled in a timely fashion.

One challenge of the radar dwell scheduling is complex physical characteristics of the phased array antenna. Scheduling of a radar dwell means transmitting a radar beam to the specified direction, waiting for a round-trip delay, and receiving the return signal. Since the round-trip delay is known by the target range [4], several radar dwells can be interleaved together. Figures 1-(b) and (c) compare nointerleaving and interleaving cases of three radar dwells J 1 , J 2 , and J 3 in Figure 1-(a), each of which is released at time 0 and has transmission time of 1, waiting time of 3, and receiving time of 1. In the no-interleaved scheduling, the total

div.p: schedule time is 15. On the other hand, interleaving greatly saves the schedule time and as a result the total schedule time is 7. However, such intensive interleaving is not always possible due to physical constraints such as transmitter duty cycle (TDC) budget and energy budget [2,12,4]. Such physical constraints limit the cumulative transmission time and energy consumption within a given length of time to prevent overheating transmitters and overloading the prime power generator. Interleaving consumes the TDC and energy more intensively for a given time and thus can be a burden to the physical constraints.

Another challenge is the dynamic workload. Due to the dynamic arrivals and departures of targets, the amount of radar dwells to be scheduled dynamically changes. In addition, as a target moves, the required sampling rate dynamically changes. This also causes the change of radar dwell workload.

Due to such physical characteristics and dynamic workload, scheduling radar dwells and providing the predictability is not trivial. In this paper, we propose a set of techniques for radar dwell scheduling to achieve the following objectives:
• taking best advantage of radar dwell interleaving to improve the overall system utilization,
• satisfying physical constraints, i.e., TDC budget and energy budget, and
• providing predictability in a way that helps radar operator's decision in overloaded situations.

To achieve these goals, we propose a novel concept of schedulability envelope. The schedulability envelope is a quantitative abstraction of complicated radar dwell scheduling that will be used for efficient schedulability check. The schedulability envelope is designed offline considering the radar dwell interleaving and physical constraints. It guarantees the system schedulability as long as the system workload state is inside the envelope. Thus, the online admission phase can determine the schedulability by simply checking the system workload state. Also, the envelope provides a clear picture about which subset of radar tasks is schedulable in overloaded situations, which helps the radar operator choose important ones considering dynamic engagement scenarios.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows: The next section describes the radar dwell scheduling problem in more detail. We also present our overall approach to the problem. Section 3 describes the offline design of schedulability envelope. Section 4 explains our online phase procedures, that is, online admission control and online radar dwell scheduling. Section 5 describes our experimental results. Section 6 summarizes the related work. Finally, Section 7 concludes this paper.

div.head: Problem Description, Assumptions, and Overall Approach
div.p: In a multi-function radar system, there are three types of tasks -search, confirmation, and track tasks. The search tasks monitor the surveillance space periodically to detect a new target. Once a new target is detected by a search task, a confirmation task is created to confirm whether the target is a critical one. If the target is confirmed to be critical, a track task is created and it periodically samples the target location to follow the trajectory.

The search tasks are static because they keep monitoring the entire surveillance space with a predefined period while the system is working. Each confirmation task is an one-time job that transmits and receives a radar beam to get a detail look for the confirmation. A track task is semi-periodic in the sense that it is created and destroyed dynamically, and during its life time, works like a periodic task except that its sampling period may change when there is a significant change in target speed and range. For the sake of explanation, we shall focus on track tasks under the assumption that a certain amount of resources is reserved for search and confirmation tasks by using periodic and aperiodic servers [13,6], respectively. However, the techniques proposed in this paper can be applied for search and confirmation tasks in the same way.

Each track task can be modeled as an end-to-end task [3,14] whose first subtask is executed on the processor (RCCradar control computer and DSP -digital signal processor) and the second subtask is executed on the antenna. The first subtask processes the previous radar return signal, estimates the next target position, and issues a radar dwell command to steer the radar beam to the estimated position. The second subtask steers the radar beam direction, transmits a radar beam to the direction, receives the reflected beam from the direction, and finally gives the received return signal back to the first subtask. All these should be completed within a sampling period, which is the end-to-end deadline. For the end-to-end deadline, we assume that the intermediate deadlines are assigned to the subtasks using a deadline assignment algorithm [14,9]. Also, we assume that a non-greedy synchronization protocol [3,14] is used between the processor and antenna in a way that makes periodic release of radar dwells. Thus, we can regard each subtask as an independent task on each resource. Scheduling of the first subtasks on the processor has been studied in [7,5,11]. Our focus is the scheduling of the second subtasks called radar dwell tasks on the antenna.

A radar dwell task, or simply a task, is denoted by a 3tuple (J, p, d) where J, p, and d are the dwell pattern, sampling period, and deadline, respectively. A dwell pattern J is denoted by a 5-tuple (T, W, R, P T , P R ) where T is the radar beam transmitting time -called Transmitter Duty Cycle (TDC), W is the waiting time, R is the receiving time, and P T and P R are power levels for transmitting and receiving the radar beam, respectively.

These parameters are determined by radar experts considering the target's physical properties and the target range [10,4]. For example, if radar experts classified targets into three types -missiles, hostile airplanes, and friendly airplanes, and discretized the target range into three precision regions -normal, precision, and high-precision regions, there can be 9 task groups (for missiles in normal region, missiles in precision region, hostile airplanes in normal region, etc.) with different parameters. From now on, by a task group, we mean the set of tasks with the same parameters. We denote the total number of task groups by K.

Dynamic arrivals and departures of targets will change the number of tasks belonging to each group. Also, as a target comes closer crossing over the region boundaries -for example, from normal region to precision region, its track task requires more timing resource changing parametersfor example, requiring higher sampling rate. This implies that a track task changes its belonging group when the target crosses over the region boundaries. Considering all such dynamics, the system workload state at any time instant can be represented by the number of tasks in each group. Formally, the system workload state at time t can be represented by a K-tuple (n 1 (t), n 2 (t), • • • , n K (t)) where n i (t) is the number of tasks in the i-th group, Group-i. We assume the deadline monotonic (DM) priority assignment [1] where a task with a shorter deadline is assigned with a higher priority. Thus, the K-tuple representing a system workload state is assumed to be sorted in DM order, that is, the deadline parameter of Group-i is shorter than that of Group-j if i < j. All tasks in Group-i have higher priority than those in Groupj. Tasks in the same group are assigned with priorities in FIFO (First-In-First-Out) order.

When scheduling the radar dwells from the tasks in the system, we have to satisfy the physical constraints, i.e., the transmitter duty cycle (TDC) budget and energy budget. The TDC budget denoted by T DC th is defined as the maximum allowable average TDC over a specified averaging time base A, generally one second [2]. The average TDC at time t denoted by T DC(t) is defined as cumulative TDC duration over the time interval of [t -A, t]. With these definitions, the constraint can be formally defined as follows:
T DC(t) ≤ T DC th for every t.

Similarly, the energy budget denoted by E th is defined as the maximum allowable average energy consumption over the specified averaging time base A. The average energy consumption at time t can be similarly defined and denoted by E(t). Thus, the formal description of the constraint is
div.formula: E(t) ≤ E th for every t. (2
div.p: With this setting, the problems we are planning to handle are as follows.

(1) how to maximally interleave radar dwells satisfying physical constraints. Interleaving significantly saves the time consumption but increases the TDC and energy consumption for a given time interval. Our goal is to find a solution such that the time saving by interleaving can be maximized while keeping the TDC and energy consumption under the thresholds.

(2) how to efficiently check the schedulability of the system. Due to dynamic arrivals and departures of tasks and occasional changes of task parameters, the efficiency of the schedulability check is essential. Since the actual dwell scheduling is very complex due to interleaving and physical constraints, taking care of such details in online schedulability check is not practical. Thus, we need an abstraction that hides the details of scheduling and provides a simple measure of schedulability.

(3) how to provide the flexibility to the radar operator. In case that not all tasks are schedulable, the radar operator may want to choose an important subset by considering dynamic engagement scenarios. For this, it is important to efficiently provide schedulable subsets to help operator's dynamic decision. Also, the online schedule should be easily adapted to operator's decision. For such flexibility, a dynamic scheduling policy needs to be considered rather than a static scheduling policy like cyclic executive.

Our overall approach to these problems consists of three phases: 1) offline design of schedulability envelope, 2) online admission control, and 3) online schedule of radar dwells of admitted tasks. In the offline design phase, we estimate the maximal interleaving satisfying physical constraints, and conduct the schedulability analysis on every possible workload state to find the boundary states from which the system becomes unschedulable. Figure 2 shows an example of boundary states denoted by big-dots when the number of task groups K is two. Applying a regression technique to the boundary states, we find a K-dimensional surface (2dimensional curve in Figure 2) represented by
This is the closed-form schedulability envelope that guarantees the schedulability as long as the system state
div.formula: (n 1 , n 2 , • • • , n K ) is inside the envelope, that is, f (n 1 , n 2 , • • • , n K ) ≤ 0.
div.p: The online admission control checks the schedulability of dynamically arriving tasks using the schedulability envelope. In traditional real-time scheduling literature, we want to guarantee a task will meet every deadline forever. However, in radar systems, target's sampling period may change from time to time and targets come and go. Thus, a more meaningful guarantee is a finite-time window guarantee. That is, we admit a new task if it is schedulable for a finite time window from the current time. Thanks to the simplicity of the schedulability envelope, we can efficiently check the schedulability for the finite time window. In Section 4.1, we will explain how the finite-time window based admission can improve the system utilization while providing good enough predictability to the radar operator.

The online scheduler schedules the radar dwells based on the deadline monotonic scheduling with a simple exponential averaging algorithm (called a constraint filter) to maximally interleave dwells without violating the physical constraints.

div.head: Offline Design of Schedulability Envelope
div.p: This section explains our offline phase to design the schedulability envelope, which will be used in the online phase. The first step is to check the schedulability for each system workload state to find the boundary states from which the system becomes unschedulable. Then, the second step is to apply a regression technique to the boundary states to find a closed-form schedulability envelope.

div.head: Schedulability analysis for a system workload state

In order to take into account the dwell interleaving in the schedulability analysis, we need the task phase information, which is however unknown in the offline design phase. Fortunately, we can control the task phases at runtime due to the nature of target detection and tracking of surveillance radar systems. A target is detected by a horizon search task from a very long distance as shown in Figure 3 [4]. After the detection, the target will be flying in the TWS (Track While Search) region for sometime (at least 214 sec under the example setting of Figure 3). In the TWS region, the required sampling rate is pretty low and comparable to the search rate, and hence the tracking can be maintained by search tasks without creating a separate track task, which is called the Track While Search (TWS) mechanism [4]. With the help of the TWS mechanism, it is fine as long as we can start the separate normal track task at sometime before the target actually moves into the normal tracking region. Likewise, we can control the actual time when the task changes to the precision and high-precision track task sometime before the earliest possible boundary crossing times.

Based on this observation, we assume that all tasks in the same group are phase synchronized. Also, we shall consider that only radar dwells from the same group are interleaved. Under the assumptions of same group phase synchronization and interleaving, we can check the schedulability of individual task groups from the highest priority group Group-1 to the lowest one Group-K. div.p: By using the schedulability analysis explained above, we can find boundary states from which the system becomes unschedulable. The boundary states are depicted in Figure 2 as big-dot states when the number of task groups K is two. Generally, when the number of task groups is K, we can regard each boundary state as a K-dimensional data point. div.head: Online Procedures
div.p: In this section, we explain the online admission control procedures for targets dynamically entering and leaving the system. Also, we explain the online dwell scheduler that actually schedules radar dwells generated from admitted tasks.

div.head: Admission control
div.p: With the schedulability envelope designed in Section 3, we can efficiently determine whether a new target can be admitted without violating the system schedulability. Specifically, if the system state is
when a target is detected and the target belongs to Group-i, the target can be admitted if the state after admitting the target, i.e.,
div.formula: (n 1 , • • • , n i + 1, • • • , n K ) is inside the envelope.
div.p: However, one problem is that the task may change its belonging group from Group-i to Group-i and in turn to Group-i as the target moves through the normal tracking region, precision tracking region, and high-precision tracking region as shown in Figure 3. It is too pessimistic to assume that the target is in the high-precision region with the highest sampling rate from the beginning, because the task will consume much less timing resource with lower sampling rates while it is flying in the normal region (at least 142 sec in Figure 3) and precision region (at least 71 sec in Figure 3).

Fortunately, we can estimate the worst case target movement assuming the direct flight of the target with the maximum speed as shown in Figure 3. As a result, we have a sequence of three time windows, each of which represents the time period while the target will be flying in normal, precision, and high-precision regions, respectively. We call the sequence of windows a target profile. Figure 7 shows an example of a target profile assuming one target type (e.g., missile) and three tracking regions (e.g., normal, precision, and high-precision). Targets in Group-1, Group-2, and Group-3 correspond to missiles in high-precision, precision, and normal regions, respectively. Based on the worst case estimation of target movement detected at time t 0 , the target profile indicates that t 1 , t 2 , and t 3 are the earliest times when the target can cross the normal, precision, and high-precision region boundaries. The height of each window represents the amount of timing resource required by the corresponding task.

Figure 7 also shows the current system profile that represents the system-state-change estimation based on the target profiles already admitted into the system. By adding the new target profile to the current system profile, we can get a new system profile. The simplicity of schedulability envelope allows us to efficiently check the schedulability for each window of the system profile.

More aggressively, we can admit the new target if the system is schedulable within a finite time period, called finitetime guarantee window, not necessarily forever. The length G of the finite-time guarantee window is specified by the radar operator. In Figure 7, the new target is admitted since the system state is inside the envelope within the finite-time guarantee window.

One problem of this aggressive admission is that the system may become unschedulable from a certain time point and hence some tasks may be dropped to retain the system schedulability. In spite of such potential drops, the rationale of the finite-time guarantee window based admission can be explained as follows. First, the drop may not actually happen if some existing targets leave the system before the system becomes unschedulable. Thus, it is too pessimistic to reject a target concerning far future. Second, the radar operator can have G-time ahead warning for candidates of potential drops. The guarantee window slides with the time t as shown in the bottom of Figure 7. When the end of the guarantee window slides into the point where the system state is outside the envelope, the radar operator is warned with a candidate of drop determined by system's pre-programmed dropping policy 1 . If the drop candidate is a critical one considering the current engagement scenario, the operator can point other less critical targets to be dropped so that the critical one can be included in the schedulable subset. Every time the operator points a less critical target, a schedulability check is required to see whether the critical target becomes schedulable. Therefore, the simplicity of our schedulability check with the schedulability envelope is essential for this process.

With this finite-time guarantee window based admission, we can improve the overall system utilization by more aggressively admitting targets while providing good enough predictability, G-time guarantee window, so that the operator can have a freedom of dynamic decision making during the G-time guarantee window. Even if some targets are dropped due to the overload, they are controlled drops chosen by the radar operator.

Since we use a dynamic scheduling policy, not a static cyclic executive schedule, the schedule automatically adapts to online system state changes determined by dynamic arrivals and departures of targets and by the operator's decisions in overloaded cases.

div.head: Experimental Results
div.p: This section compares the proposed method with two alternative scheduling methods: 1) no-interleaving and 2) best-effort. The no-interleaving method does not interleave radar dwells and performs admission control assuming nointerleaving. On the other hand, the best-effort method admits all track tasks without checking the schedulability and does best-effort to interleave as many dwells as possible checking physical constraints online. The best-effort method is the one used in traditional multi-function phased array radar systems [2].

To simplify the comparison, we consider only one target type with maximum speed of Mach 4. However, to model the task parameter change according to target range, the target range is discretized into three regions, i.e., normal, precision, and high-precision regions whose boundaries are 500 km, 300 km, and 200 km, respectively. As a target crosses over the boundaries, its track task changes to normal track 1, which is mainly based on the parameters reported in [10,12]. The deadline is set to be equal to the period to focus on the scheduling effect on the antenna. We use two sets of TDC and energy budgets to consider both of less constrained and more constrained situations. The first set Set 1 assumes that TDC and energy budgets are 600 ms and 2500 J, respectively, for the averaging time base A = 1.0 sec. The second set Set 2 assumes 400 ms and 2000 J, respectively.

Figure 9 shows the boundary states (above) and the corresponding envelope (below) for the less constrained situation. We can observe the regression penalty in the area where the number of precision targets is from 125 to 150. Figure 10 shows the same for the more constrained situation. Since the TDC and energy budgets are tighter, the possible interleaving is limited and thus the size of envelope is smaller than that of Figure 9.

In order to see the online performance, we simulated dynamic targets. The dynamic arrivals and departures of targets are modeled with Poisson arrival with average rate λ and the exponential life time with average l. We perform the experiment changing λ from 0 to 3 per sec with fixed average life time l = 300 sec. For each λ, we run the simulation until 10,000 targets enter and leave the system. Targets are assumed to move according to the worst case scenario, that is, direct flight to us with the maximum speed.

We use three performance measures: 1) the average number of targets admitted, 2) the target drop probability (target drops may happen if we use the finite-time guarantee window), and 3) dwell deadline meet probability.

Figure 11 shows the results when the TDC and energy budgets are less tight (Set 1 ). As increasing the target arrival rate, the average number of targets admitted by the nointerleaving method increases but is saturated at 50. However, our approach (see our-∞) can admit significantly larger number of targets (more than 90) by taking advantage of interleaving. If we more aggressively admit the targets using the finite-time guarantee window, the system utilization can be further improved. When the length of finite-time guarantee window is 100 sec (see our-100) and 50 sec (see our-50), we can track up to 110 and 120 targets, respectively. Such improvement by the finite-time guarantee window is possible at the cost of potential target drops. However, the target drop problem is not serious. When the length of finite-time guarantee window is 100 sec, no actual drop has been observed. Even for 50 sec finite-time guarantee window, the drop probability is very small (less than 0.5%). Furthermore, all targets that actually be dropped are controlled-drops that are deemed to be less important by the radar operator during the guarantee window. The best-effort method keeps admitting targets without checking the schedulability and thus the number of targets in the system linearly increases as increasing λ. However, it cannot guarantee the deadlines of radar dwells. As a result, the deadline meet probability significantly drops when the arrival rate becomes larger than 0.3 per sec as we can see in the bottom-most graph of Figure 11. In contrast, our approach and no-interleaving assure 100% guarantee of deadlines for the track tasks admitted into the system.

Figure 12 shows the same graphs when the TDC and energy budgets are tighter (Set 2 ). Similar trends are observed except that our performance improvement in the sense of the average number of targets is limited since the tighter TDC and energy budgets limit the maximum number of dwells that can be interleaved.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Many recent studies [7,5,11] have dealt with radar system design problems using real-time technology. For example, Kuo, Kuo, and Chang [11] formalize the workload of typical radar systems as periodic and aperiodic real-time tasks and propose effective task allocation and scheduling algorithms to process the tasks in a real-time fashion. They also provide a way to estimate the system capacity, which is essential to determine the necessary amount of resource to meet the system specification in terms of workload. In [5], Chang, Chen, Chen, and Huang model each task in a radar system as a sequence of jobs with precedence relations and contending hardware resources such as digital signal processors, communication channels, and memory. To schedule these jobs within deadlines using as less resources as possible, they propose a scheduling algorithm that effectively resolves resource contention. However, most of studies handle the scheduling problem on RCC or DSP not radar dwell scheduling problem on the antenna.

Traditional radar dwell scheduling takes a best-effort approach that tries to schedule as many radar dwells as possible while checking physical constraints with constraint filters every time it tries to schedule a radar dwell [2]. However, it does not provide a sound theory about the schedulability and thus the performance prediction mainly relies on extensive simulation and radar operators' experience.

Kuo, Chao, Kuo, Chang, and Su [10] propose a rate-based approach to scheduling radar dwells in a real-time fashion. It reserves radar resources for tasks necessary for the minimal radar operation. During the runtime, each dwell's virtual deadline is computed based on the reservation ratio and radar dwells are scheduled by the EDF algorithm. This approach guarantees the minimal radar operation and tries to maximize the overall radar performance. However, the physical characteristics of antenna like interleaving and TDC and energy budgets are not addressed.

To the best of our knowledge, the template-based dwell scheduling method proposed by Shih et. al. [12] is the only technique that can provide the predictability of radar dwell scheduling considering those physical characteristics. The technique finds a cyclic executive schedule, called a template-schedule, assuming a statically given set of tasks. For the given set of tasks, the template-schedule works fine. However, it has a flexibility problem. Depending on dynamic workload and engagement scenarios, the radar operator needs to choose important radar tasks dynamically. In this sense, a dynamic scheduling policy is preferred to give the freedom of decision making to the radar operator and decide the schedule online adapting to the operator's decision. There has been no research on dynamic radar dwell scheduling that can provide both predictability and flexibility considering the physical characteristics.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: In this paper, we propose novel techniques for scheduling radar dwells considering physical characteristics of phased array radar. In order to take care of complex physical characteristics such as interleaving, TDC constraint, and energy constraint, we propose a notion of schedulability envelope. The schedulability envelope is designed offline by taking care of all the physical characteristics. The envelope guarantees the schedulability of the system as long as the system workload state is inside the envelope.

With the envelope, our approach efficiently checks the schedulability online for the admission control. We perform more aggressive admission control based on the finite-time guarantee window. Such aggressive admission further improves system utilization while providing predictability and flexibility to the radar operator. The online scheduler based on DM scheduling using constraint filters can guarantee the schedulability for all tasks admitted into the system.

Although this paper focuses on radar dwell scheduling on a phased array radar system, the notion of schedulability envelope can be generalized. The nice thing of schedulability envelope is to hide details of complex scheduling and hence provide only a quantitative abstraction for an efficient schedulability check. Therefore, the concept can be applied for other complex real-time applications where tasks are dynamically created and thus efficient admission control is essential. We plan to extend the proposed techniques to more challenging problems such as cooperative target tracking of distributed radar systems and advanced radars with multiple antennas whose beams can be steered individually.
